title: 'Solar panels are pushing it': White House UAP adviser Avi Loeb unravels 1998 KY26 mystery, fires back at NASA chief
excerpt: In an intriguing assertion, Avi Loeb proposes that the celestial body known as 1998 KY26 may actually be a relic of Soviet engineering instead of an asteroid. He attributes its unexpected acceleration towards Earth to sunlight bouncing off its solar panels, citing its glossy appearance and a similar path to Phobos 1.
content:
1998 KY26, the rocky body that is accelerating through the solar system in a way that gravity alone can't dictate its path, and Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb, who argued it is a lost Soviet spacecraft, now thinks it's getting the unexpected push from the Sunlight.

The tooth-shaped object, measuring about 36 feet across, which NASA believed to be an asteroid, has puzzled astronomers because of its unusual acceleration. Loeb, who chairs the White House and defense UAP (Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena) Science Advisory Council, believes 1998 KY26’s unusual trek could be explained if the object is actually Phobos 1, a Soviet spacecraft launched in 1988 towards Mars whose mission failed because a mistyped software command was sent from Earth.

In a November 14 social media post, Loeb described it with the title: “Mysterious space object accelerates towards Earth as scientists debate”. It led to a massive debate about what type of object it is, an asteroid or something else entirely.


— ProfAviLoeb (@ProfAviLoeb)

In a subsequent interview on Fox News, which he transcribed and published on Medium, he explained why it's a Soviet spacecraft and how the spacecraft's solar panels could be responsible for the mysterious acceleration.


How solar panels could be pushing the mysterious object

According to Loeb, sunlight reflecting off the solar panels of Phobos 1 could generate enough pressure to alter the object’s trajectory. It is similar to how a solar sail, which uses the momentum from the absorbed sunlight to propel a spacecraft through space.

Also Read: Asteroid-hunting telescope spots a supernova explosion while it is still getting brighter

Loeb and his co-authors, Adam Hibberd and Adam Crowl, calculated that the reflection of sunlight from Phobos 1’s solar panels could explain the acceleration seen in 1998 KY26.

“The sunlight reflecting off these solar panels is pushing them, just like a sail on a boat,” Loeb explained in his interview.

Why does Avi Loeb think 1998 KY26 could be a Soviet spacecraft?

Loeb's hypothesis is based on similarities between 1998 KY26 and the lost Phobos 1 spacecraft. First, he and his collaborators found that the object's orbital trajectory is similar to that of the Soviet probe.

He also has an explanation for how the object looked like a piece of rock rather than a spacecraft, as he is proposing. “We don’t have an image of it. The image you saw is just a reconstruction from a radar that is not very accurate. But the size of the object is comparable to that of Phobos 1 and it is very shiny,” he explained.

He then cited its reflectivity, which is approximately 52%, meaning it reflects more than half of the sunlight falling on its surface. That is way higher than the roughly 5% reflectivity Loeb cited as typical of asteroids.

Another unusual feature that caught his attention is the object’s rotation every five minutes.

“In this case, we’re seeing a very shiny object, and moreover it’s spinning every five minutes, and if this was a collection of rocks that are glued together by ice, they wouldn’t stick together at such a high spinning rate,” Loeb concludes.

Japan's spacecraft will no longer visit the mysterious object

Japanese space agency, which had plans to land its Hayabusa2 spacecraft on the 1998 KY26, had canceled its proposed path, meaning scientists would lose an opportunity to examine the mysterious object up close.

Loeb, however, is hopeful that the scientific community can know more about 1998 KY26 in the future. “But now the Japanese decided not to visit this object, so unfortunately, we will not have that opportunity,” he said, adding, “I hope that next year, we'll have additional data from the Webb telescope that will settle the issue, and that is the way science is done.”

Loeb’s tirade with NASA

At the beginning of the interview, he pushed back against the claim made by NASA’s Administrator, Jared Isaacman, that it's being tracked by some of the “UAP community” who think that the object is making “unusual maneuvering” in space.

“First, a few corrections. This object was not monitored by UAP enthusiasts. It was monitored by astronomers,” Loeb said. He later added, “It's not done by NASA's administrator saying conclusively that he knows the answer. That's not the way to make progress. The way to make progress is to collect data by NASA's Webb telescope, rather than follow NASA's administrator.”
